sections.heading: Turning features on and off
sections.text: Every background output has its own switch in **Settings → Features**, and a tab stays empty until its feature is on and its source is connected. This page covers the switches, what depends on what, and how to read the status line an empty tab shows.

sections.heading: What the switches do
sections.text:
Settings → Features lists each feature with a description, a cost badge (None, Light, Medium, Heavy) and a switch. The badge is a fixed estimate of how much AI the feature spends per cycle, not live usage. Targets and Assistant Chat are marked **Core**: they have no switch.

- **Off means no work, not no data.** An off feature makes no AI calls and writes nothing new. What it already produced stays and stays readable.
- **On resumes from now.** Turning a feature back on does not process the time it was off, so there is a gap. It is the same for a feature you never turned on before.
- **Changes apply on Save.** Flip switches, then press **Save** at the bottom. Watchtower applies them and restarts the background sync once.
- **Turning off asks about dependents.** If other enabled features read from this one, a dialog offers "Disable only …" or "Disable … and N dependents". Nothing else is switched off silently.

Setup picks the starting set from your goals; see [Set up Watchtower](../start/setup.md).

sections.heading: What feeds what
sections.text:
| Feature | Cost | Feeds into |
|---|---|---|
| Attention detection (no AI) | None | Briefing |
| Knowledge search (no AI) | None | |
| Confluence in search (no AI) | None | Knowledge search |
| Slack Digests | Heavy | Tracks, People Cards, Ideas, Briefing |
| Stream Digests (mail and Jira) | Medium | Ideas, Attention detection |
| Tracks | Heavy | Briefing, Memory |
| People Cards | Medium | Briefing, Day Plan |
| Ideas & Decisions | Medium | |
| Reaction Commands | Medium | |
| Memory (off by default) | Medium | Briefing, Day Plan |
| Daily Briefing | Light | Day Plan |
| Day Plan | Light | |
| Next Step Suggestions | Medium | |
| Automations (own switch) | Medium | |
| Claude plan limits (no AI) | None | |

Tracks and People Cards read what Slack Digests writes, so with Slack Digests off they have nothing to work on. Memory has an **Advanced** section with switches for each source and each place memory is used.

sections.heading: Why a tab is empty and what its status line means
sections.text:
An empty tab shows an icon, a title ("No briefings yet"), one sentence on what will land there, a status line and at most one button. It is one of these, checked in this order:

| Status line | Means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Off — Turn on** | The feature is off. | **Turn on** switches it on at once and restarts the sync once, without going through **Save**. |
| **Connect Slack to get this** (or "a calendar", "Jira", "Jira or mail", "a source") | The source it reads is not connected. | Connect it in **Settings → Connections**. |
| **Preparing now** | Its job is running; the sync's progress follows. | Wait. |
| **Didn't work yet — retries automatically** | Its last run failed; the first line of the reason follows. | Nothing: the next cycle retries. |
| **Starts after the first sync** | Slack is connected and its first sync has not finished. | Wait; a first sync usually takes 3 to 5 minutes. |
| A time: "Within ~15 min", "After this sync", "Today at 08:00", "Tomorrow at 08:00", "In about a day", "In about 6 h" | When it runs next. | Wait. |

Once the tab has content, the empty state goes away, even if a newer run is still going.

**Turn on** works one feature at a time. If another is still turning on you see "Another feature is turning on — try again in a moment". If the restart fails the feature stays on, the reason shows under the button, and the button becomes **Try again**.

Which source each feature waits for:

- Slack Digests, Tracks, People Cards and Ideas need Slack.
- Stream Digests need Jira or mail.
- Briefing, Day Plan, Memory and Attention detection accept any connected source.
- Calendar needs a calendar.

Briefings, Day Plan and Inbox also need Watchtower to know who you are. Until a source supplies your identity they show no time at all; see [Sources and accounts](sources-and-accounts.md#why-watchtower-needs-to-know-who-you-are).

Briefings and Day Plan offer **Change the hour**, which opens Settings → Features, where the hours are **Briefing Hour** and **Generate at hour**. Before that hour the status reads "Today at 08:00" (your hour). On a brand-new install the first briefing and first day plan do not wait for it.

sections.heading: After you connect a source
sections.text: Watchtower may open "Turn on related features?" listing features the new source can feed that are still off. **Turn on** enables them and restarts the sync once; **Not now** leaves them.

sections.heading: What each source loads
sections.text:
| Source | What is loaded for the older days |
|---|---|
| **Slack** | Messages, then channel digests and daily rollups for those days |
| **Gmail, IMAP** | Messages; Gmail also gets its mail digests, which feed Ideas |
| **Jira** | Nothing to fetch, because the first Jira sync is a full scan; the month is mined for Ideas |
| **Calendar** | Not needed: 30 days of events are re-synced every cycle |
| **Confluence, meetings** | Not needed |

Muted channels and one-to-one messages are not digested during backfill.

sections.heading: What one sync cycle does
sections.text:
A small background program, the daemon, runs a cycle every 15 minutes (**Settings → System → Sync → Poll Interval**). A cycle also starts when the daemon starts, when the Mac wakes from sleep, and when you press **Sync Now** in the menu bar. The daemon keeps running when you close the window and stops when you quit the app.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Slack sync] --> B[Reaction commands]
  B --> C[Calendar, mail, Jira, Confluence]
  C --> D[Digests]
  D --> E[Tracks and rollups]
  D --> F[People cards]
  E --> G[Attention detection]
  F --> G
  G --> H[Stream digests and ideas]
  H --> I[Memory and next steps]
  I --> J[Briefing and day plan]
  J --> K[History backfill]
```

Each step runs only if its feature is on and its source is connected. A step that has nothing to do writes nothing, which is why some tabs stay quiet. If the Slack sync fails, the later steps still run on the data already stored.

sections.heading: Sources and accounts
sections.text: A source is an account Watchtower reads from. You connect them in **Settings → Connections**, and almost every feature is only as full as the sources behind it. You can connect several accounts of the same kind.

sections.heading: What each source gives
sections.text:
| Source | Where | What Watchtower takes | What reads it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Slack** | Connections → Slack | Messages, mentions and threads of the workspaces you connect, plus your own reactions | Digests, Tracks, People, Catch Up, Attention detection, Reaction Commands |
| **Google** | Connections → Google | Calendar events and the Gmail inbox, switched separately per account | Calendar, meeting prep, Day Plan, Briefings, Attention detection, Stream Digests, Ideas, Search |
| **Email** | Connections → Email | New mail from an IMAP or Outlook mailbox | Search, Catch Up, Attention detection |
| **Calendar** | Connections → Calendar | A CalDAV account or an ICS feed | Calendar, meeting prep, Day Plan |
| **Jira** | Connections → Jira | Issues, boards, sprints, releases and comments of a Jira Cloud site; Confluence spaces you pick under the site | Targets, Boards, Workload, Blockers, Search, Ideas |
| **Linear** | Command line | Issues of the teams you select, with `watchtower linear add` | Identifies you as the owner. No tab shows Linear data |
| **Quick Connections** | Connections → Quick Connections | Nothing is synced. The assistant can call an external tool server (MCP) you add, only when you ask in chat | The AI Chat. See [Quick Connections](../features/quick-connections.md) |

Slack is read-only. The assistant sends a Slack message only after you approve it, and Slack may ask you to reconnect once to grant that permission.

sections.heading: What removing an account does
sections.text:
It depends on the source. **Remove** always stops syncing and deletes the sign-in from your Mac.

- **Slack and Jira:** the data already synced stays: messages, digests, issues, boards.
- **Google, Email and Calendar:** the mail and calendar events synced from that account are deleted from the local database (a Google account keeps events tied to a recording or recap). Digests, briefings and other AI results built from them stay.

**Known issue:** the confirmation dialog for Google, Email and Calendar says synced data is kept, but it is deleted. If you need the mail or events, do not remove the account; use its **Enabled** switch where there is one, or remove it only after you have what you need. Slack and Jira do keep their data.

sections.heading: Why Watchtower needs to know who you are
sections.text:
Briefings, Day Plan and Inbox are about you, so they need your identity before they run. Watchtower takes it from the first source that can supply it, in this order: Slack account #1 (if you remove it, another workspace does not take over), the first Google account, the first enabled Jira site, the first enabled Linear account. Other accounts then add details such as your email or Jira id.

With none connected, Briefings and Day Plan say "Connect Slack, Google, Jira or Linear so Watchtower knows who you are", and those three never run. Connecting any one fixes it. A freshly connected Jira site can show this message for a moment, until Jira reports who you are.

sections.heading: Agent analytics
sections.text: Agent analytics reads the history of the Claude Code sessions that ran in a workbench folder and totals their tokens, cost, tools and errors. It is for the person who wants to know what their agents cost and did. It is a command-line feature with no screen.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
You turn analytics on per workbench. Watchtower then reads the transcript files Claude Code keeps under `~/.claude/projects/`, picks the ones that belong to the workbench folder (or one of its git worktrees, including worktrees that cleanup has removed) and stores one row per API call, tool call, skill and error in the local database. It copies no prompt or reply text, only counts and a pointer back to the file.

Each API call counts once, even when a resumed or forked session replays it. The earliest session owns a replayed call.

Cost is computed when a call is stored, from a built-in price table. A model the table does not know costs 0 and is counted as estimated.

When the table changes, older rows are re-priced from their stored tokens. Claude Code's own cost figure is kept per session so you can compare.

Once on, the background daemon keeps the numbers current: each cycle it reads only new lines, for up to 30 seconds.

The history already on disk is loaded when you turn the feature on. Turning it off keeps what was stored. Deleting the workbench keeps it too, and a new workbench on the same folder picks it up again.

Only Claude Code transcripts in `~/.claude` are read. Codex sessions are not.

sections.page_title: Writing and changing things from the AI Chat
sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
**A proposal, not an action.** A write tool never acts by itself. Calling it records a proposal and shows a card saying what it wants to do and why. **Approve** runs it once; **Reject** discards it.

A failed card offers **Retry**, and a done card links to what was created or changed. Proposals left from an interrupted reply gather at the bottom of the chat, and proposals from other places (reactions, automations, a workbench terminal) wait in the Inbox.

**What needs a click.** Anything that writes outside your Mac always waits for Approve, whatever the settings: every Jira tool, Slack send, Confluence edits. Two tools, `create_idea` and `remind_me`, run at once by default and just show what they did. **Settings → Profile → Assistant tools** lists every write tool with **Run without approval in:** checkboxes per place it is offered. External tools stay locked to Approve there.

**Where each tool works.** Slack send and `connect_jira_board` are for the main chat (Slack send also from a workbench terminal and automations). Confluence reading and editing work in the main chat and a target's chat. Draft-only chats (meeting, track, idea) offer no proposals at all.

sections.heading: Why use it
sections.text: You ask "what did we decide about the payments rollout?" and get an answer drawn from Slack, mail, Jira, meetings and digests, with the sources one click away. Nothing is pre-loaded into the conversation, so a question about your schedule or a colleague works the same way: the assistant looks it up when you ask.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
**Where answers come from.** The assistant searches everything Watchtower synced and indexed (Slack, mail, Jira with comments, calendar, transcripts and recaps, digests, decisions, ideas). That search follows the Knowledge search feature switch. Each answer folds its steps into "Worked for 12s · 4 steps", and a line below it opens the **Sources** panel, grouped by Slack channel, Jira project, Confluence space, mail, meetings and other.

**Providers.** The pill in the composer picks Claude, Codex or Ollama and a model; **Auto** is the provider's configured strong model. Claude streams text live and shows steps. Codex and Ollama answer in the same chat but may show the reply all at once, may show no steps, and cannot read images or PDFs.

**Warm sessions.** Up to three conversations keep a live assistant process, for ten minutes of idle time, so the next reply starts fast. A fourth conversation waits for a free slot; a running reply is never cut off to make room.

**Memory.** When the Memory feature's **Chat surface** switch is on, the assistant starts each chat with a short map of what it remembers and can look things up. See [Memory](memory.md).

**Other assistant chats.** The same chat component appears in a target's **Assistant** tab, the track chat, an idea or decision, a recording's **Chat** tab, an automation's **Change in words**, and the setup assistant in Settings. They have no attachments, @-mentions or branches.

Only the main chat, the target chat and the automation editor can act, through proposals. The meeting, track, idea and setup chats are draft-only: they discuss and draft but never act. At most three replies across all of them run at once; a fourth shows **Queued**.

sections.heading: The settings block
sections.text:
The top of the file holds the settings:
- **Trigger**, exactly one of: a `schedule` (five-field cron, local time), a `button` (with a label of 1 to 24 characters, and optionally `confirm`), or `manual: true` (only when you run it). The edit form calls the button option **When I press a button**; it draws no button anywhere. It only makes the recipe appear under its name in **Run Automation…** (**⌃⌘R**) and in the tray's **Run automation** submenu; with `confirm` it asks before running.
- **Permissions**, such as `gmail:read@work`, `jira:read@PAY`, `llm:light`, `llm:strong`, `tool:create_jira_issue`. Reading all Slack messages or all calendar events needs `slack:read@*` or `calendar:read@*`.
- **Outputs**, any of `inbox`, `briefing`, `report`, `target`, `slack`. Posting to Slack also needs `slack:write@<account>`.
- **Budget**: tokens (1,000 to 2,000,000) and minutes (1 to 60).
- Optionally, how many runs may overlap (1 to 4) and what to do about a missed slot.

Text outside the settings and the script is the description. The script is one block of plain, synchronous JavaScript. It can only use what Watchtower gives it: ask the assistant, read tools, a small saved state and the outputs.

sections.heading: Where recipes live
sections.text: Personal recipes sit in the `automations` folder inside Watchtower's workspace folder. The file name is the recipe's id: lower-case letters, digits and dashes. Shortcuts (symlinks) are never read; put the real file there.

sections.heading: Why use it
sections.text: You sit down at 09:00 with coffee. Instead of opening Slack, mail and Jira in turn, you open today's briefing and see the two threads waiting on you, the tasks due today, yesterday's decision in a channel you don't follow, and a note that a colleague's activity dropped. Each line links to the digest, track, target or person it came from.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
One briefing is made per calendar day, by the background sync. It is generated at or after the briefing hour (default **08:00**), not at that exact minute: if the Mac was asleep at 08:00, it comes on the first sync cycle after you wake it. Sync cycles run every 15 minutes by default.

| Condition | Why |
|---|---|
| **Daily Briefing** is on in Settings → Features | The switch for the whole feature |
| An account that tells Watchtower who you are | Slack account #1, else your first Google account, else the first Jira site with a known owner, else the first Linear workspace |
| Something to summarise | Channel digests or the daily rollup, tracks, your targets, attention items, Workbench activity or automation notes |
| Fewer than three failed attempts today | After three failures it gives up until tomorrow |

The very first briefing on a new install skips the hour and comes in the first cycle that has something to summarise. If there is nothing yet, nothing is stored and the next cycle tries again.

A briefing has up to five sections, plus today's calendar:

- **Needs Attention**: unanswered mentions, DMs and mail to you, updated tracks, overdue or blocked targets, new red flags. Workbench activity (a blocked target, open asks, unread agent comments) can appear here, labelled *Workbench*.
- **Your Day**: your targets and tracks for today.
- **What Happened**: notable events from recent channel digests. Notes your automations left for the briefing are folded in here, labelled with a gear and the automation's name.
- **Team Pulse**: people signals such as activity spikes or drops and new red flags.
- **Coaching Corner**: communication and process tips.

Rules you teach through [Catch Up](catch-up.md) feedback are applied to the briefing too.

sections.heading: Calendar and meeting prep
sections.text: The **Calendar** tab puts your meetings and recordings into one timeline, and prepares you for a meeting from what Watchtower already knows about the people in it. It works with Google Calendar and with CalDAV or ICS calendars.

sections.heading: Why use it
sections.text: You have a 1:1 in ten minutes and no idea what is open between you and that person. **Prepare** reads your Slack, Jira, tracks and people cards for the attendees and gives you talking points, open items and a short list of things to look at first. After the meeting, the same row holds the recording and its recap.

sections.heading: Reminders
sections.text:
Before each meeting a notification fires, 5 minutes ahead by default. When the event has a conference link it carries **Join** and **Join + Record**. While the app is open, a banner at the top of the window shows the same countdown with **Join** and **Record**.

If a recording linked to an event is still running 2 minutes after the event ends, a "Meeting ended — still recording" notification with **Stop recording** appears and repeats every 10 minutes. It ignores the reminder switch and the minutes, and only **Pause notifications** silences it. Pre-meeting reminders are held while paused and sent again if the meeting is still ahead when you turn it off.

sections.heading: Using it
sections.text:
1. Open the **Calendar** tab and click an event. The detail pane shows the agenda and attendees.
2. Click **Prepare**. The prep opens in the pane; **Refresh** makes a new one.
3. To steer it, type into **Your Notes** and click **Regenerate with notes**.
4. Click **Join** to open the meeting link. If **Auto-record on join** is on (the default, under **Settings → Meetings**) and nothing is recording, Join also starts a recording linked to the event.
5. Click **Record** for the event itself, or **Record** in the list header for a meeting that has no event.

To change reminders, go to **Settings → Features → Notifications**: **Meeting reminders** and **Remind before meeting** (0 to 60 minutes; 0 is **Off**).

sections.heading: Why use it
sections.text: You come back after a week away with hundreds of unread messages. Instead of scrolling channels, you build one recap for the week: a TL;DR, a handful of topics with their sources, the decisions made, and a short **For you** list of mentions, DMs, mail and tasks aimed at you. Then you press **I'm caught up** and the next recap starts from there.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
A recap is built only when you ask for it. The daemon never builds one for you.

- **Window.** **Auto** runs from the end of the last recap you marked caught up to now. With none, it covers the last 24 hours, and it never reaches back more than 31 days. The other choices are **Today**, **Yesterday**, **3 days**, **Week**, or **Range** with your own from and to (neither can be in the future).
- **Material.** The recap reads Slack and stream digests, meetings and transcripts, decisions, attention-detection items, tracks and targets for that window.
- **Top-up.** When the window ends within five minutes of now, the digests for the part not yet covered are refreshed first. A failed top-up never fails the recap.
- **One AI call** composes the recap. Every source link in it is checked against what was gathered, and a link that doesn't exist is dropped.

The tab shows when any of Attention detection, Slack Digests or Stream Digests is on and any source (Slack, mail, Jira or a calendar) is connected. **For you** is only as good as Attention detection, which needs no AI and runs every sync cycle.

sections.heading: Build a recap
sections.text:
1. Pick a window in the left column. Under **Auto** a caption names the start.
2. Click **Build recap**. The recap reads "Building the recap…" until it is ready.
3. Click a recap in the history list to read it. Older recaps stay when a new build fails.

A recap shows a TL;DR, **What happened** (topic cards with **Sources** that expand in place), **Decisions**, **Meetings** and **For you**. A window with nothing in it says "Quiet — nothing happened in this window."

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
**A channel gets a digest when it has new human messages.** After each sync cycle the daemon summarises every channel with messages its last digest has not covered. Each channel keeps its own position, so a failed or skipped channel is offered again next cycle.

Left out: muted channels, one-to-one DMs (group DMs are kept), and channels with only bot traffic. A mostly-bot channel is digested around the human replies.

**Trickle channels wait.** A channel digested less than 30 minutes ago with fewer than 10 visible messages is skipped until the next cycle. On a fresh install the first run reads the first sync's window (**Initial History Days**, 3 days when set up in the app).

**Daily rollups combine channels.** Once at least two channel digests exist for the same UTC day, the daemon writes one **Daily** digest across channels, and rewrites it when a newer channel digest lands. A day with one channel digest gets no rollup. After 3 failed attempts in a day the daemon stops retrying the rollup until the next day.

**Mail and Jira are digested too.** Stream digests summarise new Gmail threads and changed Jira issues per account, at most every 6 hours by default. They need **Stream Digests** on and a connected account, not Slack.

Meeting recaps appear in the same feed once a recording has one.

**Decisions are mined, not typed.** While summarising Slack, mail, Jira and meetings, the AI also extracts decisions. The Ideas pipeline (every 6 hours by default) merges repeats into one entry and keeps its source mentions. Decisions are born settled: **active**, with no review step.

sections.heading: Why use it
sections.text: You open the app after a meeting and want one answer: what is waiting for me? Home puts the recap you haven't read, your next meeting, pending approvals, today's briefing, your own targets and questions from coding agents in one column. Nothing here is built by Home itself, so there is nothing to wait for.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
Home only reads what the rest of the app has already produced, and refreshes about every 30 seconds. A Today card appears only when it has something to show, and only when its tab is visible: a card for Inbox, Calendar, Briefings or Catch Up disappears with that tab.

| Card | Shows | Opens |
|---|---|---|
| **SINCE YOU WERE AWAY** | The newest finished Catch Up recap you haven't marked caught up, with its TL;DR | Catch Up |
| **NEXT MEETING** | The next event starting within 24 hours: time, up to two attendees, "Prep ready" when prep exists | That event in Calendar |
| **WAITING ON YOU** | The three newest proposals, failed actions and due reminders, with the total | Inbox |
| **BRIEFING** | The first line of today's briefing | The briefing |
| **MY TARGETS** | Up to five of your own targets that are overdue, due today or in progress (never a Workbench board's) | The target |
| **AGENTS WAITING** | The three oldest questions and review requests from Claude Code or Codex sessions, with the workbench | That session |

With nothing to show, Today says "Nothing needs you right now." If a card can't be read it is skipped and the others still show. If none could be read, Today says "Couldn't read today's items — see the log."

sections.heading: The menu on the left
sections.text:
The menu lists Home, Targets, Tracks, Workbench, Automations and Calendar first. Below them are three collapsible sections:

- **FOCUS**: Catch Up, Briefings, Day Plan, Inbox, Ideas.
- **EXECUTION**: Project Map, Releases, Blockers, Workload.
- **INSIGHTS**: Digests, People, Memory, Statistics.

AI Chat and the TOOLS (Search, Boards, Usage, MCP Server) sit at the bottom. FOCUS starts open and the other two start folded; your own folds are remembered.

- **⌘B** folds the menu into a narrow icon rail and back. In the rail each section is one group icon that opens its tabs in place.
- Right-click a tab inside a section and choose **Hide**. It moves to that section's **HIDDEN** list, where **Show** brings it back.
- A tab appears only when its feature is on in Settings → Features and a source it needs is connected. For example Calendar needs a calendar, the Jira tabs need Jira, and Statistics needs Slack or mail.
- Until Slack, mail and Jira are all connected, a quiet **+ Connect …** line at the bottom names what is missing and opens Settings → Connections. Its **×** hides it for good. A connected calendar counts as mail here.
- Badges show what waits: unread briefings, proposals and due reminders in Inbox, ideas to review, one for a recap waiting for **I'm caught up**.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
The registry is filled in two steps, both by the background sync.

1. **Cheap pre-digests.** Slack digests and meeting recaps already pick out ideas and decisions. Mail and Jira get their own digest passes over recent threads, issues and comments. That pass is the separate **Stream Digests** feature, which runs about every 6 hours.
2. **Consolidation.** About every 6 hours (Settings → Features → **Ideas**, **Mining interval (hours)**, 1 to 48), a stronger AI pass reads only the new material and your recent verdicts. It proposes new ideas or attaches a repeat mention to an existing one.

It needs **Ideas & Decisions** on in Settings → Features (on by default). For mail and Jira ideas, Stream Digests must also be on. The daemon's regular pass looks only at recent activity; use **Find Ideas** to reach further back.

A mention of something you rejected, dropped or put on **Not now** brings it back into **For review** with the reason "brought up again". An exact repeat of a mention it already has does not.

sections.heading: Inbox
sections.text: The Inbox is a short queue of things waiting for your decision: reminders that came due, actions the assistant proposed, and notes from your automations. It also hides the machinery that spots what is aimed at you, which feeds Catch Up and the briefing.

sections.heading: Why use it
sections.text:
You see a Slack message you can't deal with now and react with an alarm clock. Tomorrow at 09:00 it comes back in the Inbox as a reminder with a link to the message. Another reaction turns a thread into a draft Jira issue, and it waits in the Inbox until you click **Approve**.

Nothing lands here on its own: every card exists because of something you did.

sections.heading: Let the phone do more
sections.text:
Two switches under Settings → **Workbench** on the phone:

- **Start sessions from this phone** lets you start a session from a target. It runs the Mac's default agent.
- **Type into sessions from this phone** lets you send a line to a running session. The Mac must also approve: the phone row on the Mac shows **Asks to type into sessions**, and **Allow…** grants it. **Revoke** takes it back.

A permission prompt in a session is never answered from the phone; the session shows **Needs approval on the Mac**.

sections.heading: Meeting recording
sections.text: Watchtower records a meeting on your Mac, transcribes it on-device, and writes a recap with action items you can turn into targets. It captures your microphone and the call's audio together, with no virtual audio device. It needs macOS 14.4 or later.

sections.heading: Capture
sections.text:
**Record** captures the microphone and the system audio (the other participants). The first time, macOS asks for two permissions: microphone, and system audio recording. While you record, a pill at the bottom right of the window shows the elapsed time and **Stop**, whatever tab you are on.

After **Stop**, the recording joins a queue, and each queued recording gets its own pill: "Transcribing 2/5", "Identifying speakers…", "Summarizing…".

You can start a new recording while an old one is processing. Only one transcription runs at a time, so the new one keeps capturing and its live panel reads "Waiting for previous transcription… live transcript will catch up."

If the call goes quiet, you get a warning. When nothing has come from the call for over 2 minutes after it was heard, the pill shows **No call audio** in orange and a notification fires. It usually means the output device changed.

The recording's detail later notes the gap, such as "No call audio from 15:29 to the end".

When headphones or AirPods connect or disconnect, the capture reattaches to the new device about a second later. Turn this off with **Follow audio device changes** in **Settings → Meetings**.

sections.heading: Transcription is local
sections.text:
Audio never leaves your Mac. Only the transcript text goes to your AI provider, for the recap.

Pick the **Engine** in **Settings → Meetings**. Only engines available on your Mac are listed:

- **WhisperKit (Whisper)**, the default, with the **Large v3 Turbo (recommended)** model, and **Qwen3-ASR** transcribe while you record, as long as **Live transcription** (on by default) is on.
- **Parakeet v3 (NVIDIA)** and **Apple Speech (macOS 26+)** transcribe after **Stop** and show no live text meanwhile.

The model downloads once. With the **Meetings** goal chosen at setup, it downloads in the background after the first sync, or after 10 minutes, whichever comes first. Otherwise it downloads at your first recording or dictation, and a pill shows progress with **Retry** if the connection drops.

**Preload model before meetings** (on by default) loads the model about 5 minutes before a calendar meeting starts, so **Record** starts at once.

sections.heading: What a recording produces
sections.text:
After the transcript is saved, the recap and chapters are generated on their own. A transcript under 200 characters is saved without them. Speaker labels are `[Я]` for you, from the microphone channel, and `[Speaker 1…N]` for others, with on-device speaker separation.

Each recording has four tabs:

- **Recap**: a summary, then chapters with decisions, action items and open questions. **Target** turns an action item into a target. **Follow-up draft** writes a message in your voice; it is shown to copy and is never sent.
- **Notes**: **Generate** writes publishable meeting notes. Edit them in place (they autosave), then **Copy**.
- **Transcript**: utterances with speaker and time. Click a speaker label to hear samples and name them.
- **Chat**: talk to the assistant about this meeting.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
**Plain files you can read.** The memory is markdown files in a git repository in your workspace folder (`memory/`). The files are the memory; the app's database only keeps a search index, which can be rebuilt from them at any time. Open the folder in Obsidian or any editor if you like. Before each run Watchtower saves your manual edits as a separate "owner edit" entry, so nothing you wrote is overwritten and history shows who changed what.

**How it fills itself.** Each daemon cycle, after inbox detection and the ideas phase, one consolidation pass seeds skeleton pages (a person needs about 20 messages in the last 30 days) and extracts notable episodes from channel history in bounded chunks, so a long backlog is worked off gradually. While the history backfill of a new source is still running, memory waits and does nothing, so expect no pages for the first stretch after connecting a source. Every message link is validated before a note is written.

**Beyond Slack.** In **Settings → Features → Memory → Advanced** each switch below is off by default.

- **Semantic tier**: rewrites entity pages as episodes arrive, merges duplicates, archives cold history into rollups, and forms **beliefs** ("Alice owns the deploy pipeline") whose confidence rises and falls with evidence. Reflection, belief changes in the briefing, and "remember this:" all need it.
- **Gmail source**: each email thread becomes one episode; senders become person pages (matched to Slack colleagues by email).
- **Calendar source**: each ended meeting becomes one episode, with its recap folded in when one exists. Capture happens on the first memory run after the meeting ends.
- **Jira source**: episodes from Jira issues.
- **Chats source**: lets a target's or track's chat pin a fact. Start a line with `remember this:` (or `remember:`); the rest becomes your own recorded statement. Without the prefix a chat turn is treated as drafting and never becomes memory. It also needs the **Chat surface** switch and the Semantic tier.
- **Targets & Tracks mirrors**: each target and track gets a page with status, next step and an **Open loops** list, kept in sync and cleared when done. Nothing is written back into your targets.

**Where memory reaches you.** Five **surface** switches decide whether memory may show up elsewhere:

- **Chat surface**: the AI Chat starts with a short map of what memory holds and can look things up.
- **Briefing surface**: the briefing may add a short *Memory revisions* note when a belief clearly changed. Nothing worth saying, nothing shown.
- **Reflection surface**: about once a week the assistant reviews its own history and marks beliefs that keep flip-flopping as disputed. It never changes a confidence by itself.
- **Day Plan surface**: folds open loops from memory into the day plan. It has little to add until Targets & Tracks mirrors is also on.
- **Meeting Prep surface**: adds what memory knows about each attendee, framed as the assistant's notes. An attendee with no page is skipped.

sections.heading: Where the mic button appears
sections.text:
A mic button sits next to three kinds of fields: every assistant chat input (including the setup assistants), the new-idea sheet, and a recording's **Notes** tab.

In a chat input, your words land exactly as transcribed. In the idea sheet and **Notes**, a light AI pass removes filler words and false starts, and shapes the text for where it goes (a title and body for an idea). A **Cleaned** chip with **Raw** shows for 5 seconds so you can swap back to what you actually said.

If you dictate into a field that already has text, the new text is added after it.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
A workbench has four parts:

- **The folder.** Any folder; the workbench takes its name. Watchtower sets the folder up for the agent with a skill, hooks and a local connection to the board. All of it is local to your Mac and excluded from git.
- **The board.** Targets as a tree: a feature, its tasks, their status and comments. The agent reads and writes it through Watchtower's tools, and you edit it on screen. See [Board and targets](board-and-targets.md).
- **Sessions.** Claude Code or Codex running in an embedded terminal in that folder. Each session reports its state, so a dot tells you whether it works, waits or has finished. See [Sessions](sessions.md).
- **Asks.** When the agent needs a review, a check or a decision, it files an ask and keeps working on what doesn't depend on you. See [Asks](asks.md).

Nothing here changes your own terminal workflow. A session started in your own terminal app sees the same board.

sections.heading: How the answer reaches the agent
sections.text:
Your answer is saved first. Then one line is typed into that session's terminal and sent, for example "Ask #12 answered (review: approved) — read it with get_ask 12 using the watchtower-workbench skill." If the agent is still working, Claude Code queues the line for its next turn.

Watchtower is careful not to talk over you:

- If a permission prompt is waiting, nothing is typed into it. The line **Answer saved — it goes to Claude once the permission prompt is resolved** shows, and the answer follows afterwards. **Dismiss** cancels the sending and gives the answer to the agent in the session's next brief.
- If Claude Code's input already holds unsent text, the answer is typed but not sent: **Answer typed into the terminal — press Return to send**.
- If the session is not running, nothing is typed. The agent reads the answer when the session starts again.
- If the agent withdrew the ask or replaced it with a newer round while you answered, nothing is sent and your draft is kept (**Discard draft** drops it).

sections.heading: Use the keyboard
sections.text:
Press **⌃⌘A** (Workbench › **Show Waiting for You**) anywhere in the workbench window to put the keyboard on the oldest ask. It is the only key that takes the keyboard from the terminal. After that:

- **J** / **K** move between asks. **Return** opens one.
- **1**–**3** answer a Quick ask with that button.
- In the drawer, **Tab** moves over the questions and steps, **1**–**9** pick an option or mark a check step, and **N** / **P** step through a review's margin comments.
- **⌘Return** presses the main button. **⌘⇧Return** presses **Request changes** on a review.

The single keys act only while nothing else has the keyboard. Letters work by key position, so they work on any layout.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
The **FILES** section at the bottom of the sessions panel lists the folder. A file opens in the **Files** pane in an editor with tabs. A single click opens a preview tab that the next click replaces; a double click, or your first edit, keeps it. Folders such as `.git` and `node_modules` are not listed.

Files carry git marks (modified, added, untracked, deleted, conflicted). When the session you look at works in a git worktree, the viewer follows it to that worktree, with its own tabs. See [Worktrees and cleanup](worktrees-and-cleanup.md).

Edits save themselves about a second after you stop typing, and at once when you switch tab. Watchtower never saves over a version it has not seen. If the file changed on disk meanwhile, a banner offers **Reload from disk** or to keep your edit. A file deleted under your edits is only written back when you choose to.

sections.heading: Diff review
sections.text: Diff review lets you read what an agent session changed, comment on lines, and send your comments back to the agent as one round. You use it when a session says it is done and you want to check the code, not the story.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
**Review Changes** in a session's row menu opens the **Changes** pane and starts a round. Watchtower snapshots the folder's working tree (tracked and untracked files, not ignored ones) and compares it with a base, the point where the branch left the default branch. The snapshot only writes git objects. It touches no branch, no index and no file.

The pane has a file list, a diff, and a list of comments. Files show added, modified, deleted or renamed, their line counts and a **Viewed** checkbox. Lockfiles, generated files and very large files are folded by name. Binary and oversized files show a placeholder.

A round moves through three states: you collect drafts, **Send review** stores the round, and the agent reads it with its `get_review` tool, which marks it delivered. Watchtower then puts one line into the session, `Review round #N sent (n comments) — read it with get_review N using the watchtower-workbench skill.`. The agent sees your comment text, the quoted lines and where each sits.

sections.heading: Using it
sections.text:
1. Row menu, **Review Changes**.
2. Click a file. Read the diff. **Inline** switches to one column.
3. To comment, select lines, right-click and choose **Comment**, type your note and press **Add**. Comments on the removed side are allowed in the **All** view.
4. Tick **Viewed** on files you have read.
5. **Send review (n)**. A banner tells you what happened to the line: "Line pasted — press Return in the terminal", "Will be sent when the agent's turn ends", or "Copied — paste it into the terminal".

A draft has **Delete**. A carried comment has **Edit** and **Resolve**, and an outdated one has **Resolve**. Resolved comments are not carried again.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
Three settings apply to every session of a workbench:

| Setting | Values | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Methodology** | `watchtower-flow` (default), `none` | `watchtower-flow` installs a second skill: features, specs and plans become targets, and work goes to `in_review` for a reviewer. `none` leaves only the core workbench skill and your folder rules. |
| **Ask guard** | `strict` (default), `soft`, `off` | What happens when the agent ends a turn with a request in plain text. `strict` sends it back until the agent files an [ask](asks.md). `soft` sends nothing back and raises the question as an ask for you; Claude Code's question dialog works while you are in the session. `off` checks nothing and allows the agent's own question tool. |
| **Finish check** | `on` (default), `off` | `on` sends back a turn that reports the work complete without calling `finish_session`. `off` skips the reminder, and an unfinished session ends as **Stopped** with no summary. |

Each setting comes from the first of three places that has it:

1. **Your setting** in **Agent Settings…**. It wins.
2. **The folder file** `.watchtower/workflow.md`, committed with the code, so a team shares it.
3. **The built-in default**.

The file is a short frontmatter of the same three keys, then free text. The text is the team's rules for agents. Every session's brief shows them, up to about 1,200 characters; longer text becomes a pointer to the file. The file is read up to 64 KiB, and a symlink or special file is ignored.

The agent never changes these settings. If anything about them cannot be read, the session runs as strict and on, never weaker.

sections.heading: Worktrees and cleanup
sections.text: Watchtower can give each agent session its own git worktree, so parallel agents never overwrite each other, and it can tidy up the worktrees and branches a finished session leaves behind. This page is for anyone running more than one agent in a repository.

sections.heading: Why use it
sections.text:
Two agents in one folder edit the same files. A worktree is a second checkout of the same repository on its own branch, so each session has its own copy.

The price is disk: one worktree with a warm build can take several GB, and each leaves a branch behind. Cleanup removes both, safely.

sections.heading: Where a new session starts
sections.text:
A plain new session, or **Work on It** on a card, starts in the folder. If a live agent already works in the folder, it starts in a new worktree instead. A worktree is a branch named `wt/<name>`, created under `.claude/worktrees/` in the repository from the folder's current commit. Uncommitted changes of the folder are not carried over.

Two overrides sit in the new-session menus and the card's **Work on It** menu: **In This Folder** and **In Its Own Worktree**. If git cannot make a worktree (no repository, no commits yet), the session starts in the folder and says why in **Started in the folder: …**.

A file named `.worktreeinclude` at the repository root lists ignored files, such as `.env`, to copy into each new worktree. Only files that match it and that git ignores are copied, as cheap copy-on-write clones.

Under **…** in the page header, **Worktree Setup Command…** sets one shell command that runs in each new worktree before the agent starts, for example a dependency install. A failure prints a line and the agent starts anyway. It does not run on resume.

A session row shows where the agent works, and **Show Worktree in Finder** opens it. Resuming a session whose worktree was deleted re-creates it from its branch. If the branch is gone too, the row says to start a new session.

sections.heading: What cleanup removes
sections.text:
Cleanup is Watchtower's own command, because an agent in auto mode is blocked from `git worktree remove` and `git branch -D`. It removes only what the session created, never a worktree or branch that holds work:

- A worktree is kept when it has uncommitted or untracked changes, is locked, is in use by a process or another session, or its HEAD is in neither the default branch nor any remote ref.
- A branch is kept when it is the default branch, is checked out anywhere, or has commits not pushed.

Each item is either ticked for removal or greyed out with the reason it is kept. Nothing is forced.

sections.heading: Using it
sections.text:
- **Delete…** on a session row (just **Delete Session** when there is nothing to clean) asks "Checking what this session left…" first. **Delete and Clean Up** removes the session and the worktrees and branches that can go; **Delete Only** leaves them. The quick ✕ and ⌘⌫ never clean up.
- **Clean Up…** in the row menu cleans up without deleting the session. Untick anything you want to keep.
- **Clean Up Old Worktrees…** under **…** in the page header lists every worktree and branch of the repository, with an owner hint. Nothing is ticked at first.
- A banner "Old worktrees use ~N GB." appears when removable worktrees exceed 1 GB. It appears once, after the page has been open for 30 seconds, and never again for that workbench after you open the sweep.
- When a session that Watchtower put in a worktree exits on its own, the same cleanup runs automatically for that worktree.

sections.heading: When it's empty or wrong
sections.text:
- **Something is "kept".** Read the reason next to it: uncommitted changes, unpushed commits and a running process are the common ones. Fix that and run cleanup again.
- **"Cleanup failed, so … was kept".** The session stays so you can retry.
- **A deleted workbench says "Kept n worktree(s) with work in them".** Those worktrees had work and are left on disk.

sections.heading: Accounts and sources
sections.text:
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `watchtower slack`, `auth` | Slack workspaces (`slack add` connects another; `auth login` connects the first) |
| `watchtower google`, `gmail` | Google accounts and Gmail |
| `watchtower imap`, `outlook` | Other mailboxes |
| `watchtower calendar`, `caldav` | Calendar events and CalDAV/ICS feeds |
| `watchtower jira`, `linear`, `confluence` | Trackers and Confluence spaces |
| `watchtower connections` | [Quick Connections](../features/quick-connections.md) |

Account groups differ: Slack, Google, Jira and Linear list with `accounts`, the others with `list`; `rename <id> <name>` exists on Slack, Jira, Google, IMAP, Outlook and CalDAV; `remove` exists on most (Outlook uses `logout`); `enable` / `disable` exist on Slack, Jira and Linear but not on Google, IMAP or CalDAV. Run `--help` on the group. See [Sources and accounts](../concepts/sources-and-accounts.md).

sections.heading: Keyboard shortcuts
sections.text: Every key equivalent in the app, by area. **Help → Keyboard Shortcuts** shows the same list in a window. On a workbench page the **Workbench** menu holds the workbench's chords and the **Navigate** menu the Files editor's; the tray's **New Voice Idea** shows ⌃⌥D. Some chords differ by tab: ⌘K is **Search chats** in AI Chat and **Go to…** on the Workbench tab, ⌘N is **New chat** in AI Chat and **New target** in Targets.

sections.heading: By area
sections.text: **Help → Keyboard Shortcuts** opens this list in a window. On a workbench page the **Workbench** menu shows the workbench's chords and the **Navigate** menu the Files editor's; the menu-bar icon's **New Voice Idea** shows ⌃⌥D. Some chords mean different things on different tabs: ⌘K is **Search chats** in AI Chat and **Go to…** on the Workbench tab, ⌘N is **New chat** in AI Chat and **New target** in Targets.

sections.heading: Waiting for You
sections.text:
Single keys work while no field, terminal or editor has the keyboard.

| Keys | Action |
|---|---|
| **J / K** | Next / previous ask (↓ / ↑ on a card) |
| **Return** | Open the ask in the drawer; in the drawer, write in the outlined field |
| **1–3** | Answer a Quick ask with that button |
| **Tab / ⇧Tab** | Next / previous question or step (drawer) |
| **1–9** | Pick that option, or mark a check step (drawer) |
| **N / P** | Next / previous margin comment (review) |
| **⌘Return** | Answer, Send or Approve |
| **⌘⇧Return** | Request changes (review) |

sections.heading: Also
sections.text: - In the sessions panel, **Tab** / **⇧Tab** move the keyboard on to the next or previous part of the window.

sections.heading: Day 4: prepare for a meeting
sections.text:
Your calendar is synced by now, so use it.

- **Try:** open **Calendar**, click an event with other people and click **Prepare**. Later, click **Record** on a call.
- **See:** talking points, open items and a **Missing Context** note for attendees it could not match. A recording gets a transcript, a recap and action items.
- **Needs:** a connected calendar, or the tab stays hidden. Recording needs macOS 14.4 or later and two macOS permissions on first use.

Details: [Calendar and meeting prep](../features/calendar-and-meeting-prep.md) and [Meeting recording](../features/meeting-recording.md).
